name: Bhaktajaneswarar Temple, Tirunavalur
deity: Shiva as Bhaktajaneswarar, the Lord of the devotees, with the goddess Manonmani
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu region, praised in the Tevaram; the saint Sundarar's birthplace (8th century); structural temple of Chola origin with later additions
dynasty: Chola origins, with additions by later dynasties
summary: Bhaktajaneswarar is the Shiva temple of Tirunavalur, the village where the saint Sundarar was born, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nadu Nadu region that also honours his parents and his foster-father among the sixty-three Nayanmars.

sections.history: Tirunavalur, anciently called Jambupuri and Tirunama Nallur, lies on the northern bank of the Kedilam river in Villupuram district. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nadu Nadu region, praised in the Tevaram, but its deeper fame is that it is the birthplace of three of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints: Sundarar himself, his father Sadaiyanar, and the chieftain Narasinga Munaiyaraiyar who raised him. The temple is believed to have Chola origins, with additions from later dynasties. Sundarar, called Nambi Arooran in the tradition, is dated to the 8th century and is the last of the three great Tevaram saints. His parents are venerated as saints in their own right, a distinction no other Nayanmar shares, and this gives the shrine a family warmth that devotees feel on entering.
sections.architecture: The temple occupies about two acres, with all its shrines enclosed by concentric rectangular walls, and a five-tiered rajagopuram marks the entrance. The sanctum of Bhaktajaneswarar, whose very name means Lord of the devotees, is accompanied by the shrine of the goddess Manonmani, who is also called Sundaranayaki or Sundarambikai. A separate shrine within the precinct honours Sundarar together with his two wives, Sangili Nachiyar and Paravai Nachiyar. Sundarar's shrine stands in the north-eastern corner. A notable detail is that Surya, who usually faces east, faces Shiva towards the west in this temple. Nearby, on the spot traditionally held to be the saint's birth house, a newly consecrated shrine to Sundarar has been raised.
sections.legends: The central story of Tirunavalur is the life of Sundarar. Born here to Sadaiyanar and Isaignaniyar, he was adopted with his parents' consent by the local chieftain Narasinga Munaiyaraiyar and raised as a prince, with all the rites proper to a young brahmin. When his marriage was being arranged, an old brahmin appeared and claimed that Sundarar was his bonded servant by a deed signed by the boy's grandfather, and the wedding was stopped. The matter was carried before the elders at Tiruvennainallur, where the old man led Sundarar to the temple and vanished within it. Sundarar understood that Shiva himself had come to claim him, and his first hymn, beginning Pitha Pirai Soodi, was the answer. From it grew a life of pilgrimage and song. The temple's older lore speaks of the nectar of the churning of the ocean from which the naval tree is said to have grown here, and of Garuda, cured of the serpent Adisesha's poison by worshipping Shiva at this place. These are told as tradition.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed here as at every Shiva temple. As the birthplace of Sundarar, the village keeps his memory with special devotion, and his Guru Puja is observed in the Tamil month of Aadi, in July or August, a time when the saints are remembered at Shaiva shrines. Confirm dates and local programmes on the spot, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: A visit to Tirunavalur is, for many devotees, a pilgrimage to the saint himself. Enter beneath the five-tiered gopuram, come first before Bhaktajaneswarar and the goddess Manonmani, and then go to the shrine of Sundarar in the north-east corner with his two consorts. Note the sun facing west towards the Lord. If time allows, walk to the new shrine at the saint's birth house, and stand a while by the Kedilam river, on whose northern bank the temple lies. The village is small and quiet, and the temple is best approached without hurry.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunavalur lies in Ulundurpettai taluk, about 25 km from Villupuram, which is the nearest large town and railway junction. The temple is reached through the village by way of the Tirunavalur Panchayat Union office, just before the bridge over the Kedilam river. Buses serve the village from Villupuram and Ulundurpettai. Chennai, around three hours or more away by road, has the nearest major airport. Confirm bus timings locally.
